\chapter{Give, Bring, Put}
\label{ch:mr-request-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for four everyday actions in Marathi -- give, drink, bring, put -- and name the Indo-European root under each.}

Complete MR-R22-request-verbs and ask, unaided, for water to be given, tea to be brought, and milk to be put down, each with the polite kripaya frame.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[deṇe]{\mr{देणे} (deṇe) — to give}

\label{lesson:MR-C22-dene}



\begin{quote}
You can already ask for a thing by naming it: \textbf{\mr{पाणी}, \mr{कृपया}.} That request has no verb in it at all. Here is the verb it was doing without.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{देणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{देणे}} — \emph{deṇe} — \textbf{to give}
\end{quote}

Asked of someone, it comes out as \textbf{\mr{द्या}} \emph{dyā} — \textquotedblleft{}give,\textquotedblright{} said the way you would say it to a person you are being polite to.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पाणी} \mr{द्या}, \mr{कृपया}.} — \emph{pāṇī dyā, kṛpayā.} — \textbf{Give water, please.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Nothing new. \textbf{\mr{द}} \emph{da} came with \emph{dhanyavād}; \textbf{\mr{े}} is the familiar \emph{e} mark; \textbf{\mr{ण}} has arrived with every \textbf{-\mr{णे}} verb so far. \textbf{\mr{दे}-\mr{णे}}. In \textbf{\mr{द्या}} the same \textbf{\mr{द}} is bound to \textbf{\mr{य}} by the halant you already write.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{देणे}} continues Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{ददाति}} \emph{dadāti}, on the root \textbf{\mr{दा}} \emph{dā-}, \textquotedblleft{}to give.\textquotedblright{} Behind that stands Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*deh\textsubscript{3}-}}, and Latin took it up as \emph{dare}. Three English words come out of that one Latin verb: \textbf{donate}, \textbf{dative} — the giving-case — and \textbf{data}, which began as \emph{data}, \textquotedblleft{}things given.\textquotedblright{} Greek's own form of the root, \emph{dídōmi}, is hiding in \textbf{antidote}: the thing given against.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{deṇe} — to give
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{pāṇī dyā, kṛpayā.} — give water, please
  \item \emph{Name:} three English words standing on the same root — \textbf{donate}, \textbf{dative}, \textbf{data}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask someone to give you water, politely. (\textbf{Pāṇī dyā, kṛpayā.}) What did Latin \emph{data} mean before it meant numbers? (\textbf{Things given}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A6\%E0\%A5\%87\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{देणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A6\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{दा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[piṇe]{\mr{पिणे} (piṇe) — to drink}

\label{lesson:MR-C22-pine}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{देणे}} is what you ask another person to do. This one is what you do yourself, with \textbf{\mr{पाणी}}, with \textbf{\mr{चहा}}, with \textbf{\mr{दूध}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{पिणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पिणे}} — \emph{piṇe} — \textbf{to drink}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{पाणी} \mr{पितो} / \mr{पिते}.} — \emph{mī pāṇī pito / pite.} — \textbf{I drink water.}
\end{quote}

The ending still declares who is speaking: \emph{-to} from a man, \emph{-te} from a woman, the same gendered present you have carried since the first verbs.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{प}} \emph{pa} you have from \emph{punhā} and from \emph{pāṇī}; \textbf{\mr{ि}} is the short \emph{i} mark that leans in front of its consonant even though the sound follows it; \textbf{\mr{ण}} closes it as always. \textbf{\mr{पि}-\mr{णे}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
When you learned \textbf{\mr{पाणी}}, you learned that it was built on \textbf{\mr{पा}} \emph{pā-}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink,\textquotedblright{} and that Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*peh\textsubscript{3}(i)-}} underneath it surfaces in English \textbf{potion}, \textbf{poison} and \textbf{symposium}. \textbf{\mr{पिणे}} is that same root standing on its own: Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{पिबति}} \emph{pibati}, \textquotedblleft{}he drinks.\textquotedblright{} So the word for water and the word for drinking are one word twice — the thing and the doing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{piṇe} — to drink
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mī pāṇī pito} or \textbf{mī pāṇī pite}, whichever declares you
  \item \emph{Run through:} the same sentence with \textbf{chahā}, then with \textbf{dūdh}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which earlier word carries this very root — \textbf{pāṇī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I drink tea\textquotedblright{} for your own gender. (\textbf{Mī chahā pito / pite.}) Which word you already knew is built on the same root as \textbf{\mr{पिणे}}? (\textbf{\mr{पाणी}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{पिणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%AC\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A4\%BF}{Wiktionary: \mr{पिबति}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āṇṇe]{\mr{आणणे} (āṇṇe) — to bring}

\label{lesson:MR-C22-anne}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{जाणे}} and \textbf{\mr{येणे}} were one root with a small piece added to the front of the second. That small piece turns up again here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{आणणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{आणणे}} — \emph{āṇṇe} — \textbf{to bring}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चहा} \mr{आणा}, \mr{कृपया}.} — \emph{chahā āṇā, kṛpayā.} — \textbf{Bring tea, please.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{देणे}} hands a thing over. \textbf{\mr{आणणे}} carries it here first.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{आ}} is the standing long \emph{ā} you write at the head of \textbf{\mr{आहे}}; then \textbf{\mr{ण}} twice, the retroflex you have been writing since the first infinitive; then \textbf{\mr{े}}. \textbf{\mr{आ}-\mr{ण}-\mr{णे}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{आणणे}} continues Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{आनयति}} \emph{ānayati}, and that word comes apart into two pieces you have both met. \textbf{\mr{नी}} \emph{nī-} means \textquotedblleft{}to lead.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\mr{आ}} \emph{ā-} means \textquotedblleft{}toward here\textquotedblright{} — the very prefix that made \textbf{\mr{येणे}}, \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} out of the bare root for going. So bringing, in Marathi as in Sanskrit, is \textbf{leading a thing toward here}: the same shape of thought, built twice with the same brick.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{āṇṇe} — to bring
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{chahā āṇā, kṛpayā.} — bring tea, please
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{dyā} and \textbf{āṇā} — handing over against carrying here
  \item \emph{Say it:} which prefix \textbf{āṇṇe} shares with \textbf{yeṇe} — \textbf{ā-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward here\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for tea to be brought. (\textbf{Chahā āṇā, kṛpayā.}) What did the root \textbf{\mr{नी}} mean on its own? (\textbf{To lead}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%86\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{आणणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A8\%E0\%A5\%80}{Wiktionary: \mr{नी}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭhevṇe]{\mr{ठेवणे} (ṭhevṇe) — to put, to keep}

\label{lesson:MR-C22-thevne}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{द्या}} hands a thing over. \textbf{\mr{आणा}} carries it here. The fourth request in this run asks for it to be set down and left there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{ठेवणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{ठेवणे}} — \emph{ṭhevṇe} — \textbf{to put, to keep}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{दूध} \mr{ठेवा}.} — \emph{dūdh ṭhevā.} — \textbf{Put the milk down.}
\end{quote}

The same verb covers keeping: what you put down and do not take back, you have kept.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{ठ}} is the breathy retroflex \emph{ṭha} — tongue curled back, then a puff. \textbf{\mr{े}} and \textbf{\mr{व}} and \textbf{\mr{णे}} are all familiar. \textbf{\mr{ठे}-\mr{व}-\mr{णे}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{ठेवणे}} comes through Prakrit \textbf{ṭhavei} from Sanskrit \emph{sthāpayati}, \textquotedblleft{}causes to stand.\textquotedblright{} Prakrit had no taste for the \emph{sth-} cluster and traded it for a single retroflex \textbf{\mr{ठ}}, which is why the Marathi word looks nothing like its Sanskrit parent — a worn-down word, the \emph{tadbhava} kind, beside the taken-up-whole kind you met with \textbf{\mr{मित्र}}.

Underneath sits the root \emph{sthā-}, \textquotedblleft{}to stand,\textquotedblright{} from Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*steh\textsubscript{2}-}}. English holds four pieces of it: \textbf{stand}, \textbf{stay}, \textbf{state} and \textbf{statue}. Putting a thing down, in this family of languages, has meant making it stand for a very long time.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ṭhevṇe} — to put, to keep
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{dūdh ṭhevā.} — put the milk down
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{dyā}, \textbf{āṇā}, \textbf{ṭhevā} in order — give, bring, put
  \item \emph{Name:} four English words standing on \textbf{ṭhevṇe}'s deepest root — \textbf{stand}, \textbf{stay}, \textbf{state}, \textbf{statue}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for the milk to be put down. (\textbf{Dūdh ṭhevā.}) What did the Sanskrit root under \textbf{\mr{ठेवणे}} mean? (\textbf{To stand}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A0\%E0\%A5\%87\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{ठेवणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%A5\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: sthā}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dyā / pyā / āṇā / ṭhevā]{Four asked-for actions}

\label{lesson:MR-R22-request-verbs}



\begin{quote}
Say the four infinitives in order: \textbf{\mr{देणे}, \mr{पिणे}, \mr{आणणे}, \mr{ठेवणे}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Answer once, then repair only the piece that went missing.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four shares its root with \textbf{\mr{पाणी}}? (\textbf{\mr{पिणे}}.) Which one is built on a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\mr{ठेवणे}}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
